text: How many authors are credited on the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need"?
options: Eight
Four
Six
Eleven
answer: Eight
explanation: Eight scientists and engineers at Google, led by Ashish Vaswani, and it is one of the most cited papers in computer science. Every large language model in production today is a direct descendant of the architecture it introduced.

source.title: Attention Is All You Need
source.label: Attention Is All You Need on Wikipedia

text: AlexNet is often called the paper that started the deep learning revolution in computer vision. What competition did it win?
options: The Microsoft COCO detection benchmark
The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
The Pascal VOC image classification task
The Stanford Visual Geometry Group challenge
answer: The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
explanation: AlexNet classified images into 1,000 categories and cut the ImageNet error rate by a margin nobody had seen before, in 2012. Before it the best entries used hand engineered features, and after it essentially everyone used convolutional neural networks.
answerAliases: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge

text: AlexNet classifies images into how many distinct object categories?
explanation: 1,000, and it is worth keeping the three numbers on this list apart. ImageNet itself has more than 20,000 categories, one million of the images have bounding boxes, and the whole database has over 14 million hand annotated images.

text: The transformer paper was written at which company?
options: DeepMind
Facebook
Microsoft
Google
answer: Google
explanation: Google, in 2017, which surprises people who assume it came out of DeepMind since that is where the successor models live. DeepMind was still running as a separate company acquired by Google in 2014, and the two did not merge until 2023.

source.title: Attention Is All You Need
source.label: Attention Is All You Need on Wikipedia

text: Word2Vec represents words as vectors using what principle?
options: Using the surrounding words to capture its meaning
Counting how often a word appears in each document
Sorting words by the first letter of their definition
Assigning each word a random position in space
answer: Using the surrounding words to capture its meaning
explanation: Distributional semantics, meaning is defined by context, so words that appear in similar places end up near each other in the vector space. That idea is the direct ancestor of every embedding in a modern language model and it is why king minus man plus woman lands somewhere sensible.

text: BERT was introduced in 2018 by researchers at which company?
options: Meta
Google
OpenAI
Microsoft
answer: Google
explanation: Google, in October 2018, and it was introduced with a paper whose full title is the acronym. It improved the state of the art for large language models immediately and is still, as of 2026, a common methodological component in NLP research.

text: The 2012 AlexNet paper depended on a large labelled image dataset that had not existed before. What was it?
options: ImageNet, a dataset of hand-labelled images built at Stanford
COCO, built by Microsoft a year later
Labeled Faces in the Wild, focused on celebrity photos
Pascal VOC, a set of 20,000 images
answer: ImageNet, a dataset of hand-labelled images built at Stanford
explanation: ImageNet was assembled at Stanford with tens of millions of hand-labelled images, and AlexNet's win in 2012 was as much a demonstration that the data existed as it was an architectural advance. Before it, the field trained on datasets like Pascal VOC with roughly 20,000 images, which is two orders of magnitude smaller.
answerAliases: ImageNet, a dataset of hand-labelled images built at Stanford

text: The 2015 paper that introduced residual networks won which competition that same year?
options: The Pascal VOC detection task
The COCO keypoint benchmark
The ILSVRC segmentation track
The ImageNet challenge
answer: The ImageNet challenge
explanation: The ImageNet challenge, in the ILSVRC series, with a network roughly twenty times deeper than the 2012 winner. The title of the paper is literally the explanation of why that was possible, since learning a residual correction is easier than learning a full mapping.
answerAliases: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge

text: The 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need threw out the recurrent encoder-decoder setup that had dominated machine translation. What did it build in its place?
options: Self-attention layers, with position added to the input
Long short-term memory cells chained one token at a time
Convolutional filters with a wider receptive field each layer
Gated recurrent units, with attention between the encoder and decoder
answer: Self-attention layers, with position added to the input
explanation: The paper describes its architecture as based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. What that bought was parallelism, because no position has to wait for the one before it, which is why a Transformer trained in days where the recurrent models it replaced took weeks.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on arXiv

answerAliases: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely

text: The 2012 AlexNet paper said its depth was what made it accurate, and that the same depth was computationally expensive. What did it name as the thing that made that depth affordable?
options: Buying a much smaller set of images to train on
Replacing the depth with a much wider shallow network
Training the network on graphics processing units
Training the network on a large cluster of server CPUs
answer: Training the network on graphics processing units
explanation: It ran on two consumer Nvidia GTX 580 graphics cards, in a bedroom, with hand-written C++ and CUDA because no GPU machine-learning framework existed yet. The hardware half of the story is the one that usually gets left out, and it is why deep learning looked practical a year before most of the field believed it was.
answerAliases: utilization of graphics processing units (GPUs) during training

text: In the 2022 InstructGPT work, reinforcement learning from human feedback rests on one step where people do the actual work. What were they asked to do?
options: Rewrite each answer by hand so the model could copy it
Rank several candidate answers the model wrote, best to worst
Write a long critique of every answer the model gave
Approve or reject each answer as a simple pass or fail
answer: Rank several candidate answers the model wrote, best to worst
explanation: The paper collects a dataset of rankings of model outputs, and those rankings train a separate model to predict which answer a person would prefer. Comparing candidates against each other is fast and consistent work for a person to do, which is exactly why this one label is so cheap and so load-bearing.

text: The 2022 chain-of-thought paper got models reasoning step by step without any fine-tuning. What did it put in the prompt to do it?
options: A few worked examples with the reasoning steps written out
A few worked examples that give only the final answer
A short list of the facts the question is known to depend on
A score for how badly the earlier attempt was graded
answer: A few worked examples with the reasoning steps written out
explanation: The method is a handful of chain of thought demonstrations supplied as exemplars, and the model copies their shape when it answers. The paper's sharpest finding is that this only pays off on sufficiently large models, which is why the same prompt helps a frontier model and does nothing for a small one.

text: Diffusion image models are described as denoising models. What is the model actually doing when it generates a picture?
options: Starting from a blank canvas and drawing the subject in one pass
Starting from a finished image and adding detail and colour back
Starting from a rough sketch and sharpening the outlines
Starting from pure static, removing a little noise each step
answer: Starting from pure static, removing a little noise each step
explanation: Training corrupts real images by adding a little more noise at every step until only static is left, and the model learns to run that backwards, peeling a small amount of noise off at a time. Because each step is a simple prediction rather than a fight between two networks, diffusion displaced GANs for image generation within a couple of years.

source.label: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models on arXiv

text: In which year was the paper "Attention Is All You Need" first published on arXiv?
explanation: The paper appeared on arXiv in June 2017, and its number 1706.03762 encodes that month. The 2015 distractor tempts people who remember the sequence-to-sequence era, but that work still used recurrence, which is exactly what the 2017 paper threw out.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on arXiv

text: Who is credited as the first author of "Attention Is All You Need"?
options: Ashish Vaswani
Illia Polosukhin
Jakob Uszkoreit
Niki Parmar
answer: Ashish Vaswani
explanation: Ashish Vaswani led the eight-author Google team, and his name comes first on the paper. The distractors are all genuine co-authors, which is why this is hard: Illia Polosukhin and Jakob Uszkoreit are the names people remember from later interviews, but neither was first author.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on arXiv

text: In BERT pretraining, what happens to some input tokens under masked language modeling?
options: They are translated into another language for alignment
They are hidden and the model must predict them from surrounding context
They are deleted from the vocabulary permanently
They are shuffled into random order to test robustness
answer: They are hidden and the model must predict them from surrounding context
explanation: About 15 percent of tokens are masked and the model predicts them using both left and right context, which is what makes BERT bidirectional. Translation is the tempting wrong answer because multilingual BERT does handle many languages, but it never translates tokens as a training objective.

text: What capability did the GPT-3 paper of 2020 most famously demonstrate at scale?
options: Performing new tasks from a few examples given in the prompt
Updating its weights from user corrections during a chat
Browsing the live web to verify facts before answering
Running compiled code in a sandbox to check its own math
answer: Performing new tasks from a few examples given in the prompt
explanation: GPT-3 showed that a large enough model can do few-shot in-context learning, adapting to a task from examples in the prompt with no weight updates. The weight-update distractor is wrong in an important way: the whole point was that adaptation happened without any gradient steps at all.

text: What did the RoBERTa paper change relative to BERT's original recipe?
options: It replaced the transformer with a recurrent encoder for longer contexts
It shrank the model to run on a single mobile phone processor
It dropped next-sentence prediction and trained longer on more data
It trained only on labelled sentiment data for sharper classifiers
answer: It dropped next-sentence prediction and trained longer on more data
explanation: RoBERTa found BERT was undertrained, so it removed the next-sentence-prediction objective, switched to dynamic masking, and trained on an order of magnitude more data. The result matched or beat BERT on GLUE without any architectural change, which is the paper's sticky lesson: the recipe mattered more than the model.

text: What unifying framing did the T5 paper introduce for NLP tasks?
options: Every task as reinforcement learning with a hand-shaped reward
Every task as retrieval from a frozen knowledge index
Every task as graph traversal over a syntax tree
Every task as text in and text out with a task prefix
answer: Every task as text in and text out with a task prefix
explanation: T5 cast translation, summarization, classification and question answering as text-to-text problems distinguished by a short prefix like translate or summarize. That single interface let one model train on many tasks at once, which is why the retrieval distractor misses the point: nothing is looked up, everything is generated.

text: How does ELECTRA's pretraining objective differ from BERT's masked language modeling?
options: A discriminator judges every token as original or replaced by a generator
A decoder reconstructs whole documents from a single summary vector
A classifier predicts the publication year of each paragraph
A ranker orders shuffled sentences back into their true sequence
answer: A discriminator judges every token as original or replaced by a generator
explanation: ELECTRA trains a small generator to replace some tokens and a discriminator to flag every replaced token, so the loss applies to all positions instead of just the masked 15 percent. That denser signal is why ELECTRA matched BERT-quality results with far less compute, and the sentence-ordering distractor describes ALBERT's objective instead.

text: How does the Vision Transformer feed an image into a transformer?
options: Compressing the whole image into one average color vector
Splitting the image into fixed patches embedded as a token sequence
Tracing object outlines into vector graphics before encoding
Stacking video frames so motion predicts the missing pixels
answer: Splitting the image into fixed patches embedded as a token sequence
explanation: ViT chops the image into patches such as 16x16 pixels, linearly embeds each one, and processes the resulting sequence exactly like word tokens. The single-vector distractor is wrong because it would discard all spatial structure, which is precisely what the patch sequence preserves.

text: The Vision Transformer paper's title says an image is worth words of what size?
options: 8x8 Words
32x32 Words
16x16 Words
64x64 Words
answer: 16x16 Words
explanation: The paper is titled An Image is Worth 16x16 Words, after its default patch size of 16 by 16 pixels. The 32x32 option is the trap because the paper also reports results at that coarser patch size, where accuracy drops exactly as you would expect from blurrier tokens.

text: What training signal did the CLIP paper use to connect images and text?
options: Human-written captions scored one image at a time for grammar
Pixel-level masks drawn by annotators around every named object
Depth sensors recording the distance of each photographed subject
Matching which of many captions belongs with which image
answer: Matching which of many captions belongs with which image
explanation: CLIP learns from 400 million image-text pairs with a contrastive objective: given a batch, predict which caption goes with which image. The pixel-mask distractor describes supervised segmentation datasets, which need expensive human labels, while CLIP's trick was learning from captions scraped from the web.

text: Which team introduced Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models in 2020?
options: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel
Ian Goodfellow and colleagues with adversarial nets
Diederik Kingma and Max Welling with variational autoencoders
Yang Song and Stefano Ermon with score matching
answer: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel
explanation: Ho, Jain and Abbeel at Berkeley showed diffusion models could generate high-quality images, kicking off the line of work behind Stable Diffusion. The Goodfellow distractor names the GAN inventors, whose adversarial training diffusion replaced, and Song and Ermon built the parallel score-based line that later merged with it.

source.label: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models on arXiv

text: What did the DDIM paper change about diffusion sampling?
options: It required thousands more steps for measurably sharper fur texture
It made sampling deterministic and work in tens of steps instead of hundreds
It replaced the neural network with a lookup of stored training images
It generated images at ten times the resolution of the training data
answer: It made sampling deterministic and work in tens of steps instead of hundreds
explanation: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models generalized the sampling process so it no longer had to be Markovian, giving the same trained model a fast deterministic sampler. Cutting hundreds of network evaluations down to tens is what made diffusion practical for interactive tools, and the lookup distractor would just be memorization rather than generation.

text: At what weight precision does QLoRA store the frozen base model?
options: 32-bit float
16-bit float
8-bit integer
4-bit NormalFloat
answer: 4-bit NormalFloat
explanation: QLoRA compresses the frozen model to a 4-bit NormalFloat format tuned to the bell-shaped distribution of neural weights, then trains LoRA adapters on top. That combination famously allowed fine-tuning a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48GB GPU, where the 8-bit distractor describes the earlier LLM.int8 approach.

text: Who introduced FlashAttention in 2022?
options: Ashish Vaswani
Tri Dao
Noam Shazeer
Llion Jones
answer: Tri Dao
explanation: Tri Dao, then at Stanford, wrote FlashAttention as an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that quickly became standard in training stacks. The distractors are all transformer-paper co-authors, which catches people who assume every attention advance came from that same team.

text: Which reinforcement learning algorithm fine-tuned the policy in the InstructGPT pipeline?
options: Q-learning
REINFORCE with human demonstrations
Deep deterministic policy gradients
Proximal Policy Optimization
answer: Proximal Policy Optimization
explanation: After supervised fine-tuning and reward-model training, InstructGPT optimized the policy against the reward model with PPO. Q-learning is the trap for readers from the games era, but it is a value-based method for discrete control, not the policy-gradient workhorse used for language models.

text: In Constitutional AI, what supplies the feedback that trains the harmlessness preference model?
options: Paid crowdworkers ranking thousands of answer pairs by taste
The model critiquing and revising itself against a written constitution
Classifiers trained on government content-moderation logs
Live user thumbs-down clicks collected from a public demo
answer: The model critiquing and revising itself against a written constitution
explanation: The model generates responses, critiques them against a written list of principles, revises them, and those self-revisions become the preference data, a setup later called RLAIF. Crowdworker rankings are the RLHF baseline this replaced, which is exactly why that distractor feels right but describes the old method.

text: What loop does the ReAct paper have the language model repeat?
options: Compress, encrypt, transmit and acknowledge each message
Draft, cite, peer-review and retract candidate claims
Write a reasoning trace, take an action, then read the observation
Sample, cluster, prune and distill a population of prompts
answer: Write a reasoning trace, take an action, then read the observation
explanation: ReAct interleaves verbal reasoning traces with tool actions such as search or lookup, feeding each observation back into the next thought. Pure chain-of-thought only reasons and pure tool use only acts, and the paper showed that alternating the two beats either alone on question-answering benchmarks.

text: Which prompt did the 2022 zero-shot chain-of-thought paper append to unlock step-by-step reasoning?
options: Let's think step by step
Answer quickly with no explanation
Repeat the question before answering
List every fact you memorized first
answer: Let's think step by step
explanation: Kojima and colleagues showed that appending this single sentence lets large models reason through problems with no worked examples at all. It is the zero-shot cousin of the few-shot demonstrations paper, and the no-explanation distractor is its exact opposite: rushing the model is what suppresses reasoning.

text: What does Toolformer teach a language model to do with APIs?
options: Hard-code one fixed call template chosen by its developers
Refuse every tool call to keep all reasoning in plain text
Download larger tools to replace its own decoder layers
Decide for itself when a call helps and which API to use
answer: Decide for itself when a call helps and which API to use
explanation: Toolformer annotates its own training text with candidate API calls in a self-supervised way, keeping only the calls that reduce its loss, so it learns when tools like calculators and search genuinely help. The fixed-template distractor describes ordinary function calling, which came later and hands that decision to the developer instead.

text: What kind of sequence model is Mamba?
options: A pure quadratic self-attention transformer variant
A selective state-space model with linear-time scanning
A diffusion sampler running noise removal over tokens
A retrieval index with no learned sequence weights
answer: A selective state-space model with linear-time scanning
explanation: Mamba makes classic state-space models input-dependent so they can select what to remember, giving transformer-quality results with compute that grows linearly in sequence length. The attention-variant distractor is the key confusion to kill: Mamba's whole point is competitive modeling with no attention at all.

text: Which lab released the original LLaMA weights to researchers in February 2023?
options: Google
OpenAI
Meta
Mistral AI
answer: Meta
explanation: Meta released LLaMA under a research-only license in February 2023, and its leak onto torrent sites days later effectively open-sourced the weights. Mistral is the trap because it later became the open-weights champion, but the company did not exist until months after LLaMA shipped.

text: What attention trick did the Mistral 7B report credit for handling long sequences cheaply?
options: Full attention over a million tokens on every layer
Attention replaced entirely by fixed random projections
One shared attention head for the whole network
Sliding-window attention with a rolling cache
answer: Sliding-window attention with a rolling cache
explanation: Mistral 7B lets each token attend to a sliding window of recent tokens, and stacking layers gives an effectively much larger receptive field at a fraction of the cost. The million-token distractor describes later long-context flagships, not this 2023 efficiency play that beat Llama 2 13B with 7 billion parameters.

text: What did the DeepSeek-R1 report claim produced its reasoning behavior?
options: Distilling answers from a much larger proprietary teacher
Hand-written rule books covering each tested science subject
Large-scale reinforcement learning that let reasoning emerge
Human annotators rewriting every wrong chain by hand
answer: Large-scale reinforcement learning that let reasoning emerge
explanation: The January 2025 report showed reasoning behaviors like self-verification emerging from large-scale reinforcement learning starting from the base model, with minimal supervised data. The distillation distractor is backwards: R1 was the model everyone else rushed to distill, not the product of it.

text: What scale did the DeepSeek-V3 report of December 2024 describe?
options: 671 billion total parameters with 37 billion active
46 billion total parameters with 13 billion active
96 billion total parameters with 12 billion active
8 billion total parameters with 2 billion active
answer: 671 billion total parameters with 37 billion active
explanation: V3 is a 671-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only 37 billion parameters per token, trained for a fraction of the cost of comparable dense flagships. The 46-billion figure is the Mixtral trap, and the active-versus-total split is the detail to remember about every MoE scale claim.

text: Which Nobel prize recognized the AlphaFold work in 2024?
options: The Nobel Prize in Physics
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
The Nobel Peace Prize
answer: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry
explanation: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared half of the 2024 chemistry prize for protein structure prediction, with the other half going to David Baker for computational protein design. Medicine is the natural wrong guess since proteins mean drugs, but the committee framed it as solving a chemistry problem.

text: What does MuZero learn that earlier game-playing systems were given up front?
options: A model of the environment dynamics for planning ahead
A database of every grandmaster opening ever recorded
A hand-coded scoring function written by game designers
A chat interface for asking humans for the next move
answer: A model of the environment dynamics for planning ahead
explanation: MuZero learns its own latent model of how the environment responds and plans with it, so unlike AlphaZero it needs no simulator or knowledge of the rules. That is why the same algorithm could play Go, chess, shogi and Atari: the dynamics model is learned from experience in each new world.

text: The 2021 Perceiver paper set out to handle images, audio and text with one architecture. How did it dodge the quadratic cost of attending over huge inputs?
options: It cross-attends the raw input into a small fixed-size latent array, then applies self-attention there
It runs full self-attention directly over the raw input bytes of every modality
It trains a separate transformer encoder from scratch for each modality
It downsamples every input to a tiny thumbnail before doing anything else
answer: It cross-attends the raw input into a small fixed-size latent array, then applies self-attention there
explanation: The input cross-attends into a few hundred latent vectors, and all the heavy self-attention happens in that small space, so cost grows with input size only through the cheap cross-attention step. Full self-attention over raw bytes is exactly the quadratic trap the paper set out to escape, which is why that option describes the problem rather than the fix.

text: What did the 2022 Perceiver IO paper add on top of the original Perceiver?
options: A contrastive loss that aligns image and text encoders
A retrieval index that fetches text chunks during generation
A flexible output query so one model can emit labels, text, pixels or flow fields
A mixture-of-experts layer that routes tokens to separate specialists
answer: A flexible output query so one model can emit labels, text, pixels or flow fields
explanation: Perceiver IO adds an output query array that cross-attends the latents, so the same encoder can produce a class label, a sentence, optical flow or raw pixels depending on the query. The mixture-of-experts distractor belongs to Switch Transformer, a different scaling story from the year before.

text: How does the 2021 RETRO model use its two-trillion-token retrieval database when generating text?
options: It copies the single closest document verbatim as its answer
It retrieves relevant chunks and cross-attends to them while predicting the next tokens
It fine-tunes its weights on the retrieved chunks before each reply
It uses retrieval only to rerank answers after generation finishes
answer: It retrieves relevant chunks and cross-attends to them while predicting the next tokens
explanation: RETRO splits both the input and its giant corpus into chunks, retrieves neighbours of each chunk, and fuses them with chunked cross-attention as it predicts. It never retrains per query, which rules out the fine-tuning distractor, and retrieval happens during generation rather than as a post-hoc rerank.

text: DeepMind's 2021 Gopher model was notable at release mainly for what?
options: Beating grandmasters at StarCraft II with no prior games
Generating images from text better than rival generators
Running on a single consumer graphics card
Its enormous dense scale, hundreds of billions of parameters, then near the frontier of model size
answer: Its enormous dense scale, hundreds of billions of parameters, then near the frontier of model size
explanation: Gopher packed 280 billion parameters into a dense transformer and matched or beat rivals on reading, fact-checking and reasoning tests. StarCraft belongs to AlphaStar, a different DeepMind project, and image generation was never Gopher's job.

text: Google's 2022 PaLM paper trained a 540-billion-parameter model on two TPU v4 pods. What system made that training setup possible?
options: Pathways, which orchestrates training across thousands of accelerator chips
A single giant graphics card holding all the weights at once
Volunteer laptops donating idle compute over the internet
A purely CPU cluster with no accelerators at all
answer: Pathways, which orchestrates training across thousands of accelerator chips
explanation: Pathways let a single system spread one model across thousands of TPU chips with clever sharding, and the 540-billion-parameter PaLM run was its showcase. No single card could hold those weights, which is what makes the lone-GPU distractor physically impossible rather than merely unlikely.

text: The 2022 UL2 paper unified pretraining objectives with a Mixture-of-Denoisers. What does that mixture combine?
options: Three separate models that vote on each answer at test time
Several span-corruption styles, from short masked spans to long aggressive ones
Human rankings mixed with AI-written critiques
Translation pairs mixed with image-caption pairs
answer: Several span-corruption styles, from short masked spans to long aggressive ones
explanation: UL2 frames every objective as corrupting spans and reconstructing them, mixing short regular gaps, longer aggressive ones and full-prefix generation so one model learns them all. The three-voting-models distractor is an ensemble, a test-time trick, while UL2 is a single pretraining recipe.

text: The 2021 T0 paper showed strong zero-shot results on unseen tasks. What fine-tuning recipe produced that?
options: Training only on labelled sentiment reviews for sharper classifiers
Reinforcement learning from live user thumbs-down clicks
Multitask training on a large collection of prompted datasets with natural-language instructions
Distilling answers from a much larger proprietary teacher model
answer: Multitask training on a large collection of prompted datasets with natural-language instructions
explanation: T0 fine-tuned an encoder-decoder on dozens of datasets, each wrapped in many natural-language prompts, so new tasks arrive as just another instruction to read. The teacher-distillation distractor describes how smaller models later copied giants, not how T0 itself learned to follow instructions.

text: The 176-billion-parameter BLOOM model was trained on ROOTS, a corpus built for the project. What made ROOTS distinctive?
options: It contained only English Wikipedia articles from a single year
It was generated entirely by an earlier language model
It held only Python code with no natural language
Web text gathered across dozens of natural and programming languages by hundreds of researchers
answer: Web text gathered across dozens of natural and programming languages by hundreds of researchers
explanation: ROOTS gathered web text across dozens of natural and programming languages through workshops of researchers who could document consent and provenance. An English-only Wikipedia scrape would have defeated BLOOM's whole multilingual purpose, and nothing in the corpus was machine-generated.

text: OpenAI's 2022 Whisper paper took an unusual approach to speech-recognition data. What did it train on?
options: Hundreds of thousands of hours of audio with transcripts scraped from the web, used with minimal cleaning
A few hundred hours of studio recordings read by voice actors
Only synthetic speech generated by a text-to-speech system
Silent video clips with no audio track at all
answer: Hundreds of thousands of hours of audio with transcripts scraped from the web, used with minimal cleaning
explanation: Whisper learned from a vast haul of weakly labelled web audio, trading curation for scale, and that robustness is why it transcribes accents and background noise so well. Studio recordings are the old supervised recipe Whisper deliberately abandoned.

text: The 2020 NeRF paper represents a 3D scene as what, so that new views can be rendered from any angle?
options: A hand-modelled mesh sculpted by artists in editing software
A neural network mapping 3D positions and viewing directions to color and density
A stack of photographs stapled together in angle order
A point cloud captured by an expensive laser scanner
answer: A neural network mapping 3D positions and viewing directions to color and density
explanation: NeRF fits a small neural network that outputs color and density for any 3D point seen from any direction, then renders views by marching rays through it. A hand-modelled mesh needs artists, which is exactly the labour NeRF removes.

text: The 2021 Masked Autoencoders paper found vision transformers learn best when pretraining hides how much of each image?
options: Masking only one pixel in twenty
Masking one pixel in four
Masking three of every four patches
Masking everything but a thin border
answer: Masking three of every four patches
explanation: Masking three quarters of the patches forces the model to reason about whole objects from slivers, and the paper showed accuracy climbs as masking rises far past the small fractions used in language. Masking almost nothing would make reconstruction trivial copying, which teaches the encoder nothing.

text: The 2020 SimCLR paper learns image representations without labels. What is its core training signal?
options: Predicting the publication year stamped on each photograph
Reconstructing every pixel of the input image exactly
Classifying each image into one of a thousand fixed categories
Pulling two augmented views of the same image together while pushing different images apart
answer: Pulling two augmented views of the same image together while pushing different images apart
explanation: Two random crops, color jitters and blurs of one image must land near each other in embedding space while other images are pushed away, and that tug-of-war alone learns features that rival supervised ones. The thousand-categories distractor is ImageNet classification, the labelled paradigm SimCLR was built to escape.

text: The 2019 DistilBERT paper compressed BERT by knowledge distillation. What was the headline trade-off it reported?
options: Ten times larger than BERT with slightly better accuracy
About forty percent smaller and sixty percent faster while keeping most of BERT's accuracy
Identical size to BERT but trained on ten times more data
A vision model that replaced BERT for image tasks
answer: About forty percent smaller and sixty percent faster while keeping most of BERT's accuracy
explanation: A student network trained to mimic BERT's soft outputs kept nearly all of its benchmark performance at a fraction of the size and latency. A larger model would be the opposite of compression, which rules out the ten-times-larger distractor immediately.

text: The 2019 ALBERT paper shrank BERT-style models with two tricks. Which pair did it introduce?
options: Factorized embeddings plus cross-layer sharing, with sentence-order prediction
Full attention replaced by fixed random projections in every layer
Removing all normalization layers and doubling the vocabulary
Training only on labelled sentiment data for sharper classifiers
answer: Factorized embeddings plus cross-layer sharing, with sentence-order prediction
explanation: ALBERT factorizes the embedding matrix and reuses the same weights across layers, then replaces next-sentence prediction with ordering two consecutive sentences correctly. Random projections describe a different efficiency family, not learned sharing.

text: The 2021 Switch Transformer paper scaled past a trillion parameters efficiently. What routing rule defines it?
options: Every token is processed by every expert in parallel
Tokens are routed by a human-written rulebook per subject
A dense feedforward layer replaces all experts at test time
Each token is routed to exactly one expert chosen by a learned switch
answer: Each token is routed to exactly one expert chosen by a learned switch
explanation: A router sends each token to its single best expert, so capacity grows with expert count while compute per token stays flat, and the paper reached past a trillion parameters that way. Sending every token everywhere would cost as much as a dense model of that size, defeating the design.

text: Google's 2021 GLaM model held over a trillion parameters across dozens of experts per layer. Why did it cost less energy to serve than a dense model of that size?
options: It deleted its largest layers before serving
It ran entirely on volunteer laptop CPUs
Only a small subset of experts activates for each token, so most weights sit idle per prediction
It answered every query from a cache of past responses
answer: Only a small subset of experts activates for each token, so most weights sit idle per prediction
explanation: GLaM holds over a trillion weights but wakes only a couple of experts per token, so each prediction costs a fraction of a dense giant's. The deleted-layers distractor confuses sparsity with amputation: the weights stay, they just take turns.

text: Besides sensibleness, specificity and interestingness, the 2022 LaMDA paper scored replies against external knowledge sources. What was that metric called?
options: Parameter count of the serving model
Groundedness, whether replies stay consistent with known sources
Tokens generated per second on a phone
Number of languages the model can translate
answer: Groundedness, whether replies stay consistent with known sources
explanation: Alongside sensibleness and specificity, the paper scored groundedness against known sources, because a chatbot that sounds right but invents facts fails exactly where dialogue matters. Parameter count is a property of the model, not a grade of any reply.

text: DeepMind's 2022 Sparrow paper built a dialogue agent that cites evidence. How did it ground its answers?
options: Live web search queries whose results the model must quote as supporting evidence
A hand-coded rulebook covering every tested science subject
Memorized passages with no live lookup at all
Paid crowdworkers rewriting every wrong answer by hand
answer: Live web search queries whose results the model must quote as supporting evidence
explanation: Sparrow issues live search queries and must support its claims with quotes from the results, with human rules shaping the ranking. Memorized passages would go stale and cannot be checked, which is why the paper insisted on browsing.

text: The 2022 InstructGPT paper reported a striking preference result. What did human labelers prefer?
options: The giant base model over the fine-tuned models in every test
A model trained only on code over every dialogue model
Random outputs over any fine-tuned model for creativity
The small fine-tuned InstructGPT model over the base GPT-3, despite having far fewer parameters
answer: The small fine-tuned InstructGPT model over the base GPT-3, despite having far fewer parameters
explanation: Labelers preferred the small aligned model's answers to the giant base model's, the result that sold the field on alignment over raw scale. The code-only distractor is backwards: general helpfulness won, not a narrow specialty.

text: The 2022 Constitutional AI paper trains a harmless assistant in two stages. What are they?
options: Pretraining on books, then deleting the safety filter
Training a chatbot, then replacing it with a search engine
Supervised learning from self-revisions, then reinforcement learning on AI-generated preference labels
Collecting user thumbs-downs, then banning those users
answer: Supervised learning from self-revisions, then reinforcement learning on AI-generated preference labels
explanation: First the model revises its own answers against the constitution and learns from those revisions, then a preference model trained on AI-labelled comparisons steers it with reinforcement learning. User thumbs-downs are the human-feedback loop this pipeline was designed to replace.

text: Besides masked language modeling, BERT's original pretraining used a second objective on sentence pairs. What was it?
options: Translating each sentence into twelve new languages
Next-sentence prediction, deciding whether the second sentence follows the first
Counting how many nouns appear in each paragraph
Reconstructing whole documents from a single summary vector
answer: Next-sentence prediction, deciding whether the second sentence follows the first
explanation: BERT learned whether sentence B actually follows sentence A, which taught it relationships between sentences rather than just words inside them. Translation is the multilingual-BERT association people reach for, but it was never a pretraining objective.

text: Why did OpenAI release GPT-2 in stages in 2019, starting with a small model?
options: Concerns about malicious uses such as disinformation, so larger versions followed months later
The larger models had failed every benchmark and were abandoned
A court order banned language models above a fixed size
The team had lost the training code and rebuilt it slowly
answer: Concerns about malicious uses such as disinformation, so larger versions followed months later
explanation: OpenAI cited misuse worries including disinformation and released progressively larger versions as the expected harms failed to materialize. Failed benchmarks would have killed the project, not staged it, which is why that distractor reverses the story.

text: The 2016 AlphaGo Nature paper combined deep neural networks with Monte Carlo tree search. What did the neural networks first learn from?
options: Only games AlphaGo played against itself from random moves
Hand-coded Go proverbs written by game designers
A database of grandmaster chess openings
Millions of positions from human expert games, before reinforcement learning self-play refined them
answer: Millions of positions from human expert games, before reinforcement learning self-play refined them
explanation: The networks first imitated millions of human expert positions, then improved through self-play reinforcement learning, with tree search guiding both training and play. Pure self-play from scratch was the later AlphaGo Zero breakthrough, not the 2016 system.

text: The 2021 DALL-E paper generated images from text with a two-stage recipe. What did it do?
options: Diffusing pure noise into pictures over hundreds of steps
Copying the closest training image for each prompt
Compressing images into discrete tokens, then training a transformer to predict them from text
Rendering 3D meshes with a physics engine, then photographing them
answer: Compressing images into discrete tokens, then training a transformer to predict them from text
explanation: A discrete autoencoder compresses each image to a grid of tokens, and the transformer learns to emit that grid conditioned on text, unifying vision and language as one sequence problem. Diffusion over noise is the rival family that later overtook this recipe for image quality.

text: DeepMind's 2022 Flamingo paper gave a frozen language model visual understanding. How did images feed into the language model?
options: By converting every picture into a long English caption first
Through a Perceiver-style resampler whose visual tokens plug into gated cross-attention layers
By retraining the whole language model from scratch on pixels
Through a retrieval index that pastes in similar photos
answer: Through a Perceiver-style resampler whose visual tokens plug into gated cross-attention layers
explanation: A Perceiver-style resampler squeezes each image into a few visual tokens that enter the frozen language model through gated cross-attention, preserving its few-shot abilities. Retraining everything from scratch would destroy the language priors the whole trick relies on.
